name: Mouth breathing correction / myofunctional therapy

card.summary: Tongue, lip and nasal-breathing exercises promoted to improve breathing and facial structure, with the facial claims resting mostly on conceptual models.
card.aka: Myofunctional therapy, mouth taping, nasal breathing
card.note: Evidence for changing adult facial structure is lacking.

quick.overview:
Mouth breathing correction covers exercises and habits meant to encourage nasal breathing and proper tongue posture, sometimes with lip taping at night. Communities link it to jaw development, facial shape and sleep apnea.
Encyclopedic sources say chronic mouth breathing in children may affect facial growth, but support comes mainly from textbooks, reviews and conceptual models.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say tongue posture and nasal airflow shape the jaws and airway. Sources describe mouth breathing as most often a response to nasal congestion, with treatment aimed at the underlying cause and building a nasal breathing habit.
quick.risks: The health effects of mouth taping have been little researched, according to encyclopedic sources. Persistent mouth breathing can reflect nasal obstruction that merits assessment.

lead: Mouth breathing correction is the practice of shifting breathing from the mouth to the nose and training the tongue, lips and jaw muscles to rest in what proponents call a proper posture. It includes orofacial myofunctional therapy (OMT), a set of tongue, lip and swallowing exercises usually taught by a therapist, as well as habits such as nasal breathing and, in some communities, taping the lips closed during sleep [1][2][3]. People pursue it in the hope of a better-defined jaw and midface, a more closed mouth at rest, and better sleep, which they also link to how rested and healthy they look.

The facial case rests on the proposal that chronic mouth breathing in children influences dental and facial growth, including a long, narrow face sometimes called long face syndrome, although Wikipedia notes the relationship may run in both directions [1]. In about 85 percent of cases mouth breathing is described as an adaptation to nasal congestion, and treatment focuses on any underlying obstruction and on building a nasal breathing habit [1]. On looksmax.org, OMT is presented as part of 'face maxxing' alongside tongue posture and jaw work [4].

Published trials of myofunctional therapy have mostly looked at sleep apnea, tongue thrust and open bite rather than facial appearance. Meta-analyses of adult sleep apnea patients report lower apnea-hypopnea index scores and less snoring and sleepiness after therapy [2][3], and small randomised trials have examined OMT in children and adults with open bite [5][6].

Beyond clinic exercises, nasal breathing became a mainstream wellness topic after James Nestor's 2020 book Breath, and mouth taping spread widely on TikTok, where its most common claims concern better sleep and oral health.[17][20] Reviews of the child-development literature report that mouth breathers differ from nasal breathers in jaw rotation and airway measurements, which is the research basis proponents cite for the facial case.[13][15]

paras: About 85 percent of cases are attributed to nasal congestion, with less common causes including antrochoanal polyps, a short upper lip that does not rest closed (lip incompetence) and pregnancy rhinitis [1]. Wikipedia classifies mouth breathing as obstructive, habitual or anatomic [1]. Enlarged adenoids can obstruct airflow and are associated with snoring and sleep-disordered breathing [1].

Interest in closing the mouth has a long lineage. Wikipedia notes that in the 19th century the painter George Catlin observed that Plains peoples preferred nasal breathing and had straight teeth, publishing a book in 1862 that was later retitled Shut Your Mouth and Save Your Life, and that yoga teacher B. K. S. Iyengar advocated breathing in and out through the nose.[1] By 1915 'mouth-breather' had become a slang insult in English.[1]

In modern orthodontics the link between airway and facial form is associated with the 'adenoid facies' concept, a long narrow face, high palate and open bite linked to adenoid-related obstruction, which a 2024 review in Frontiers in Public Health describes as a vicious cycle between mouth breathing, adenoid hypertrophy and craniofacial development.[15] John Mew and his son Mike Mew promoted tongue posture as part of 'orthotropics', and interest in the idea rose from January 2019 and spread on social media, especially in looksmaxxing communities, according to Wikipedia.[19]

Orofacial myofunctional therapy itself is taught by speech-language pathologists, dentists and other clinicians for tongue thrust, sleep-disordered breathing and tongue-tie, and the looksmaxxing forums borrow its vocabulary for appearance goals.[2][3][4][7][9] Nestor's Breath, published by Riverhead Books on 26 May 2020, reached the New York Times bestseller list and has sold more than two million copies according to Wikipedia; reviewers in the Wall Street Journal and The Spectator praised its reach while questioning its reliance on anecdote.[20]

sections.h: Proposed effects on the face and teeth
paras: Wikipedia lists anterior open bite, tongue thrusting, gingivitis and plaque among dental conditions associated with mouth breathing, and says chronic mouth breathing in children may affect dental and facial growth and contribute to a long, narrow face.[1] The article describes these as associations, with support from textbooks, reviews and conceptual or cephalometric work.[1]

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis in BMC Oral Health pooled ten studies comparing mouth-breathing and nasal-breathing children. Mouth breathers showed lower SNA and SNB angles, a steeper occlusal plane, backward and downward rotation of the mandible and maxilla, and narrower airway measures.[13] The authors read this as mouth breathing affecting facial skeletal development.[13]

A 2018 meta-analysis of three non-randomised studies (155 children) followed facial growth after surgery to relieve mouth breathing; it reported a mandibular plane angle change of about -2.1 degrees over at least a year, with total anterior face height changes that were not statistically clear, and rated the evidence quality very low.[18] Researchers on adenoid facies describe airway obstruction, perioral muscle dysfunction and malocclusion as reinforcing one another.[15]

The main approach described is treating any underlying nasal obstruction and building a habit of nasal breathing.[1] Orofacial myofunctional therapy adds exercises to optimise tongue placement and increase oropharyngeal muscle tone, typically with a therapist guiding swallowing patterns, tongue and lip strength, and breathing.[3] Looksmax.org threads describe the same elements as lips together, tongue resting against the palate and nasal breathing, and present them as groundwork for tongue posture and jaw exercises.[4]

Mouth taping involves keeping the lips shut during sleep with a strip of tape, and Wikipedia says its health effects have been little researched.[1] A 2025 systematic review in PLoS One by Rhee and colleagues screened literature from 1999 to 2024 and included ten studies with 213 patients; two reported significant improvement in apnea-hypopnea index or oxygen desaturations, others found no difference, and the authors cautioned that indiscriminate taping poses a potentially serious risk where nasal obstruction is present.[14] A 2025 scoping review in the American Journal of Otolaryngology found nine eligible studies and reviewed the first 50 TikTok videos on the topic, reporting that the common claims were improved sleep and oral health and that the literature was heterogeneous.[17] A May 2025 HealthDay report on a review of mouth taping carried the headline 'Little Benefit, Lots Of Risk'.[8]

Where congestion is the cause, treatment of the obstruction comes first in clinical descriptions. Forum users discuss nasal sprays, sleep apnea checks and surgeries such as turbinate reduction, septoplasty and maxillary expansion, and one thread warns members about empty nose syndrome as a risk of turbinate surgery.[11][12]

A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine adult studies (120 patients) reported a fall in the mean apnea-hypopnea index from 24.5 to 12.3 events per hour, along with less snoring and lower sleepiness scores after myofunctional therapy [2]. A 2024 meta-analysis of seven randomised trials with 310 patients reported statistically significant improvements in apnea-hypopnea index, sleepiness and sleep-related quality of life [3].

A 2025 randomised trial compared a palatal crib alone with a crib plus brief OMT for anterior open bite in 32 patients, measuring tongue pressure and overbite change [5], and a 2016 pilot randomised study examined OMT in children with open bite and tongue dysfunction [6]. Reviews have also looked at OMT for tongue thrust habits and for ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) [7][9].

A 2023 systematic review in the journal Children examined orofacial myofunctional therapy for craniomaxillofacial growth in children with obstructive sleep apnea and hypopnea. It retrieved 1,776 articles and included nine studies with 693 children, of which three had severe and five moderate risk of bias; it reported improved craniofacial function or morphology in most children, with larger effects for longer treatment and better compliance.[16]
Reviews of tongue-tie report that surgery is more effective than myofunctional therapy alone, with better results when both are combined.[9]

A looksmax.org thread describes OMT as the fundamentals behind tongue posture, mewing and jaw exercises and argues that an open mouth, low tongue and slack lips affect breathing, sleep, chewing and facial appearance.[4] In another thread a user describes a consultation at a clinic offering a jaw-growth device and facial exercises that compared the approach with mewing; the user questioned whether it could produce the jaw advancement he wanted, saying the clinic could offer about 4 to 5 mm.[10] Users also discuss nasal obstruction surgery and mouth taping, including a thread asking whether taping damages skin.[11][12][21]

Mewing coverage describes the broader tongue-posture trend as going viral in incel and looksmaxxing subcultures, with orthodontic bodies reporting no evidence that it improves the jaw, and with Mike Mew struck from the UK dental register in 2024.[19] Myofunctional therapy is often presented in these communities as the clinically recognised version of the same ideas, a framing that rests on the sleep and bite literature rather than on appearance outcomes.[4][2][5]

Randomised trials and meta-analyses of myofunctional therapy exist for obstructive sleep apnea, open bite, tongue thrust and tongue-tie.[2][3][5][6][7][9] A systematic review of mouth breathing in children reports skeletal differences from nasal breathers, and a review of OMT in children with sleep-disordered breathing reports improved craniofacial function or morphology.[13][16] No study found tested mouth-breathing correction or OMT for changing adult facial structure or measured appearance as an outcome. Wikipedia reports that the evidence linking mouth breathing and facial growth is largely conceptual or based on limited cephalometric work.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, myofunctional therapy is discussed as the muscle-training foundation of tongue posture and mewing, and mouth taping and nasal breathing come up as sleep habits.[4][11]

claims.claim: Open-mouth breathing and a low tongue 'sabotage' the face and airway
claims.believers: A popular thread argues that a slack mouth and weak tongue affect breathing, sleep, chewing, speech and facial look, and that OMT addresses these together [4].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says chronic mouth breathing in children may affect facial growth, with the relationship possibly running both ways and support coming mainly from conceptual and limited cephalometric work [1].

claims.claim: Myofunctional therapy can improve sleep and snoring
claims.believers: Users link nasal breathing and tongue training with better sleep.
claims.experts: Meta-analyses of adult sleep apnea patients report reduced apnea-hypopnea index, snoring and sleepiness after OMT [2][3].

claims.claim: Jaw-growth devices and exercises can move the jaw forward in adults
claims.believers: A clinic in one forum account said exercises and a device could bring 4 to 5 mm of forward movement [10].
claims.experts: No study found tested OMT for adult jaw advancement; the poster said the clinic could not promise the larger change he wanted [10].

claims.claim: Mouth taping at night improves nasal breathing
claims.believers: Users discuss taping alongside nasal sprays and sleep apnea checks [11].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says the health effects of mouth taping are little researched [1], and a May 2025 HealthDay report on a review described limited benefit and safety concerns [8].

claims.claim: Mouth breathing in childhood changes jaw and face development
claims.believers: Proponents of tongue posture and airway-focused orthodontics say chronic open-mouth posture leads to a longer, narrower face.[4]
claims.experts: A 2021 meta-analysis of ten studies found skeletal differences between mouth-breathing and nasal-breathing children; a review of surgery to relieve mouth breathing rated its evidence very low quality.[13][18]

claims.claim: Myofunctional exercises can change adult facial structure
claims.believers: Forum posts present OMT as foundational to a better jaw and face.[4]
claims.experts: No study found tested OMT for changing adult facial structure; trials examine sleep apnea, bite and tongue function, and a children's review reports improved craniofacial function or morphology.[2][3][16]

claims.claim: Mouth taping at night is safe and helpful for anyone
claims.believers: Social media videos most often cite better sleep and oral health.[17]
claims.experts: A 2025 systematic review of ten studies concluded that indiscriminate taping may carry serious risk where the nose is obstructed and that benefit needs more study.[14]

claims.claim: Nasal breathing is an overlooked basis of health and looks
claims.believers: Popular writers such as James Nestor describe a shift from nasal to mouth breathing linked to snoring, sleep apnea and allergies.[20]
claims.experts: Reviewers praised the book's reach but criticised its reliance on anecdote and limited skepticism.[20]

angle.text: Practitioners train tongue and lip muscles and nasal breathing so the mouth rests closed with the tongue up, which proponents say supports the jaw, midface and airway. People also use nasal breathing to sleep better, which affects how rested they look.
